You are about to run a complete data science workflow. You will start with a raw file on the
internet and finish with a monthly climate summary, all before you know how any single piece
works. Today you run through all of it once. Over the next eight days you will learn how each
part was built.

::: {.callout-important title="Don't panic 🚀"}
You are not expected to understand every line today. Your job is to copy code, run it, and
change one thing at a time. Our job is to show you what a workflow looks like. By next Friday
you will know how all of it works.
:::

We will use real Arctic weather data from the [Arctic LTER](https://lternet.edu/site/arctic-lter/)
station at Toolik Lake, Alaska: daily measurements from 1988 onward. This session covers the
first half of the workflow: Import, Explore, Group, and Aggregate. We skip Clean along the way,
for a reason you will see. Session 1d finishes the job with Visualize and Export, and gives the
whole workflow its name.

## How today's steps work

You are going to run code you cannot fully read yet. To make that manageable, every step of
the workflow follows the same small pattern. We chose this pattern for Day 1 to help you build
confidence before you build understanding.

Each step has up to three parts:

1. **Run it.** Copy the canonical cell and run it exactly. Everyone gets the same result, so we
   all begin each step from the same place.
2. **Change one thing.** Swap a single item from a short menu, then run it again to see what
   moves. These cells always rebuild their result from `df`, so they leave your data alone. The
   next canonical cell brings everyone back together.
3. **Say it in a sentence.** After some steps you will write one f-string that reports a number
   you just produced. f-strings are the thing you learned to write this morning, so this is
   where you practice writing for yourself.

The goal on Day 1 is to see the whole workflow and get a feel for each step. Mastering the
syntax comes later. Running working code shows you where each step lands. Changing one thing
gives you a safe way to experiment. Writing a sentence keeps you using the one skill you
already own.

## Step 1: Import 📂

**Import** means loading your tools and then loading your data.

✅ **Canonical cell. Copy and run it exactly:**

```{python}
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/EDS-217-Essential-Python/EDS-217-Essential-Python.github.io/refs/heads/main/data/toolik_weather.csv"
df = pd.read_csv(url)
```

The `import ... as ...` lines load Python toolkits under short nicknames. You will see three of
them all course long: `pd` for pandas (data), `plt` for matplotlib (plots), and `np` for numpy
(math). `pd.read_csv(url)` reads a CSV straight from the web into a **DataFrame**, a table,
which we store in `df`.

:::{.callout-note}
Today `read_csv()` needs only one thing: the `url` of a CSV file. It can do much more, and you
will learn that on Day 2.
:::

:::{.callout-tip title="🔁 Change one thing"}
`read_csv` builds a table, and you can give that table any name you like. Load the same data
into a new variable, using one name from this menu:

- `climate = pd.read_csv(url)`
- `toolik = pd.read_csv(url)`
- `weather = pd.read_csv(url)`

Your original `df` stays exactly as it was. You have simply made a second copy under a new name.
:::

```{python}
# 🔁 Example: same data under a new name. Reads url again; leaves df alone.
climate = pd.read_csv(url)
```

:::{.callout-tip title="✍️ Say it in a sentence (optional)"}
Write an f-string that names what you loaded. For example, set `dataset = "Toolik weather"` and
then print `f"I loaded the {dataset} dataset."`
:::

## Step 2: Explore 🔍

**Explore** means getting to know the table before you analyze it.

✅ **Canonical cell. Preview the first rows:**

```{python}
df.head()
```

:::{.callout-tip title="🔁 Change one thing"}
Swap `.head()` for one other no-argument view of the same table:

- `df.info()` shows the column names, types, and how many values are present.
- `df.describe()` shows summary statistics for the number columns.

Each one looks at `df` without changing it.
:::

```{python}
# 🔁 Example: a structural overview instead of a row preview. Reads df; leaves it alone.
df.info()
```

```{python}
# 🔁 Example: summary statistics. Reads df; leaves it alone.
df.describe()
```

### The health check

Before you trust a dataset, run a quick **health check**. This is a fixed phrase you will reuse
all course long. It counts the missing values in every column:

```{python}
df.isnull().sum()
```

:::{.callout-important}
Look at `Daily_AirTemp_Mean_C`. It has zero missing values, so the column we are about to
analyze is complete. A few other columns do have gaps, which is normal. We only need our column
to be clean.
:::

:::{.callout-important title="✍️ Say it in a sentence (required)"}
`df.info()` reported how many rows the dataset has. Read that number, then report it in your own
f-string. For example:

```python
n_rows = 11171          # the number info() showed you
print(f"The Toolik dataset has {n_rows} daily records.")
```

Now write a second sentence of your own, maybe about how many columns there are.
:::

## Step 3: Clean 🧹 (skipped today, and here is why)

The next step in a normal workflow is **Clean**: fixing missing values, wrong types, and
duplicate rows. Our health check already showed that `Daily_AirTemp_Mean_C` has no missing
values, so there is nothing to clean for today's analysis, and we can go straight on.

:::{.callout-note}
Enjoy this while it lasts. Most real datasets need real cleaning, and it is often the biggest
part of a project. You will spend all of Day 4 on it. Today the data came ready to use.
:::

## Step 4: Group 👥

**Group** means splitting the rows into buckets by some key. Here we bucket every daily record
by its **Month**, so all the Januaries sit together, all the Februaries, and so on.

✅ **Canonical cell. Copy and run it exactly:**

```{python}
monthly = df.groupby('Month')
```

:::{.callout-tip title="🔁 Change one thing"}
Change only the key you group by. Pick one from this menu:

- `by_year = df.groupby('Year')` buckets records by year, which gives many groups.
- `by_station = df.groupby('Station')` gives a single bucket here, because every row is the
  same station.

Both read `df` without changing it, and neither touches your `monthly` grouping.
:::

```{python}
# 🔁 Example: group by Year instead of Month. Reads df; leaves df and `monthly` alone.
by_year = df.groupby('Year')
```

## Step 5: Aggregate 📈

**Aggregate** means collapsing each bucket down to a single number. Here we take the mean
temperature within each month. Notice the two-step shape: first group, then pick a column and
average it.

✅ **Canonical cell. Copy and run it exactly:**

```{python}
monthly_means = monthly['Daily_AirTemp_Mean_C'].mean()
monthly_means
```

That gives twelve numbers, one average temperature per month, summarizing thousands of daily
records into a clear seasonal pattern.

:::{.callout-tip title="🔁 Change one thing"}
Keep the grouping and change only the column you average. Pick one from this menu:

- `monthly['Daily_Precip_Total_mm'].mean()` gives average daily precipitation.
- `monthly['Daily_AirTemp_AbsMax_C'].mean()` gives the average daily high temperature.

Store the result under a new name so your `monthly_means` stays put.
:::

```{python}
# 🔁 Example: average a different column. Reads `monthly`; leaves monthly_means alone.
monthly_precip = monthly['Daily_Precip_Total_mm'].mean()
monthly_precip
```

:::{.callout-important title="✍️ Say it in a sentence (required)"}
Look at your `monthly_means`, pick one month's value, read it off, and report it in an f-string.
For example:

```python
july_temp = 11.2        # July's value, read from monthly_means
print(f"At Toolik, the average July temperature is {july_temp} degrees Celsius.")
```

Now write one more sentence for the month you find most surprising.
:::

## 🧪 Sandbox (5 minutes)

Now poke at it yourself. Try a different column, a different grouping key, or a deliberate typo.
Errors are expected today, and they are welcome. A red error message is Python telling you
something. See what you can make happen.

:::{.callout-caution title="↩️ Canonical restart. Run this to rejoin the group"}
When the five minutes are up, run this cell to reload the data and rebuild the canonical
results. Everyone returns to the same state, ready for Part 2:

```{python}
# Restart: reload df and rebuild the canonical results
df = pd.read_csv(url)
monthly = df.groupby('Month')
monthly_means = monthly['Daily_AirTemp_Mean_C'].mean()
```
:::

## Key Points

- You ran a real workflow from start to finish: Import, Explore, Group, and Aggregate. You
  skipped Clean only because the health check proved our column was complete.
- `pd.read_csv(url)` loads a CSV from the web into a DataFrame. `.head()`, `.info()`, and
  `.describe()` are your no-argument ways to look at it.
- `df.isnull().sum()` is the health check for counting missing values.
- Grouping and then averaging turns thousands of rows into a short summary. You did it in two
  steps: first `monthly = df.groupby('Month')`, then `monthly['Daily_AirTemp_Mean_C'].mean()`.
- The change-one-thing cells always re-read `df`, so your data stays put and the group can
  always reconverge.
